content.thinking:
I'm pulling together the postmortem facts: an alert fired because spend totals weren't reconciling across shopper accounts, traced to a deploy that broke record_purchase's update to the monthly total, with the issue starting shortly after that deploy went out.

Looking at the diff, I confirm the new code drops the field that tracked month-to-date spend, so regardless of which code path a purchase takes, the monthly total stops updating entirely. Since several downstream readers — monthly statements, spend summaries, and the reconciliation check itself — rely on that stored value, shoppers would have seen understated month-to-date spending on their statements even though no purchases or charges were actually lost.

Now I'm tracing the causal chain: statements read the stored monthly total, but new purchases since onset never updated that field because revision 26f1d7e removed the month-total increment from record_purchase, and the alternate derivation path also left it untouched — so whichever code path ran, the stored total fell behind actual purchases. That revision is now live across all replicas, and I'm checking whether an earlier deploy could be ruled out given the lack of pre-onset metrics.

The oldest affected purchase, per the integrity check, dates to just after the later revision deployed, which rules out the earlier deploy as the cause since the first harm postdates it. I'm also noting zero flag changes in the hour before onset, which rules out a flag-change explanation, though I still need to check how the flag provider reads values.

The real mechanism: the revision assumed the month total would be derived from purchase history on demand, but the readers still pulled from the stored total_this_month_cents field, which went stale once that field stopped being updated — citing the docstring, schema, and usage sites as evidence, and stopping where the author's assumption can't be directly confirmed.

This confirms the cause rests on actual evidence rather than unverified reasoning. In plain terms: a code change stopped updating each shopper's running monthly total when a purchase was made, but the parts of the system displaying and checking that total still read the stale stored value, so it fell behind actual purchases. The risk is ongoing since the revision is still live everywhere, meaning the gap keeps widening with every new purchase, and there's also a concern flagged about month rollover making simple recomputation incorrect.

I should note that rollback alone likely wouldn't fix totals already written short, since the old code added incrementally — that's an inference worth flagging modestly, and F1 confirms a repair script is needed.

For contributing factors: the spend-integrity check only runs every few days, letting drift go undetected longer than necessary — more frequent or continuous reconciliation would catch it sooner. There also wasn't a test verifying reconciliation after a purchase write, which could have caught the field removal before it shipped.

F1's proposed test only covers the derive_the_month=True path, not the default record_purchase path at 26f1d7e — AI-1 partially addresses this by merging a fix to main and adding tests for derive_the_month=True, but I think a separate test covering the default path running reconcile is still needed. Lastly, nobody appears to have been paged when the alert fired, since it wasn't linked to on-call — had someone been paged, a rollback likely would've happened sooner.

For the deployment itself, the revision running (26f1d7e) wasn't on main at all, meaning it bypassed whatever review gate requiring main-only deploys would provide — had that policy been enforced, this change couldn't have reached production unreviewed.

I should also note the flag-gated month-dropping path exists on main itself, meaning even the "safe" path was broken; that's partly root cause, though I'll let AI-1 handle fixing it on main.

For action items, I'm thinking: repair the already-understated stored totals via export, dry-run the repair script, then apply it before month-end closes out.

I'm also considering that AI-2's rollback to 4c810f22 needs scrutiny — I need to check whether that revision's version of record_purchase still moves both totals correctly, since D1 only documents purchase_ledger.py as changed.

So that means the derive-the-month flag path likely still had the bug at that revision, since only the default record_purchase hunk was patched — meaning rollback alone fixes the default path but leaves the flagged path still drifting.

I should flag two actions: make sure the fix also updates the derive_the_month path before it's deployed, and keep that flag off until then, since I don't actually have visibility into its current state. I'm also considering whether the flagged path could've caused earlier incidents, but the onset timing after P2 suggests no shoppers were actually on that path yet.

For the still_at_risk note, the core issue is that the stale revision remains on all replicas, so every new purchase keeps widening the gap in stored totals, and the unfixed write path leaves things unmoved too.

Now I'm drafting the lessons-learned section, noting that Argus correctly linked the onset to the P2 deploy and reviewed its diff quickly after the alert, and that Code-Fix drafted a pull request with a test and repair script.

For what went wrong, I'm flagging that the Investigator split C1 and C2 into separate candidates even though they trace to the same change, and that the investigation only looked at record_purchase while missing the derive-the-month path, leaving the rollback recommendation incomplete.

For what went right, the stored totals already written short aren't fixed by the rollback itself, only by Code-Fix's unrun repair script, so I should note that gap.

For the lucky break, the fault was caught before the month ended, so the stored totals can still be recomputed within the same-month window F1 requires — timing worked in their favor, not the customer impact being low.

I'm being careful about assumptions: that shoppers saw the short totals on their statements is inferred from the reader logs, not an actual user report, and the flag state for derive_the_month is unverified since flags were read but never returned. For step 3's ruled-out causes, I need to cite the earlier deploy against the purchase records and the flag change against its timestamp, and I should avoid stating raw time intervals directly, using relative references instead.

For the action item, I'm drafting a test that writes current-month purchases through record_a_purchase with derive_the_month false, then asserts reconcile_monthly_totals shows no disagreement — complementing the existing coverage that only exercises the true path.

For detection, I'm proposing the spend-integrity check run far more frequently, paging on-call when SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile fires, requiring production deploys to come only from main, and running repair_monthly_totals.py in report-only mode then with --apply before month rollover.

For mitigation, once PR #342 merges I need an actual deploy of that revision, since rolling back to 4c810f2 doesn't fix the derive_the_month path, and derive_the_month should stay off for all shoppers until the fix ships. I'm mapping CF-2 to AI-1's test additions plus my own item, and confirming CF-4 is legitimate since the record itself notes the deployed revision isn't in main's history and wasn't reviewed.

Now I'm drafting the chain summary: citing the sources for step 2, then writing the symptom statement for step 1 — the mismatch between shoppers' spend totals and their actual purchases, how many totals didn't reconcile, the largest shortfall, and noting that both the monthly statement and spend summary pull from the same stored figure.

action_items.item: Add a test that records current-month and earlier-month purchases through record_a_purchase with derive_the_month false and asserts that reconcile_monthly_totals finds no disagreement, alongside the derive_the_month true cases proposed in PR #342.
Run the spend-integrity check much more often than every {A5} days, so that drift in stored totals is found soon after it starts.
Run the spend-integrity check against io-shop after every production deploy.
Route SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile on io-shop so that it pages the on-call person when it fires.
Require io-shop production deploys to come only from revisions on main.

Export the affected accounts and run scripts/repair_monthly_totals.py from PR #342, report-only first and then with --apply, and load the result back before the month rolls over. Code-Fix says the recomputed figure would be wrong after that.
Once PR #342 is merged, deploy a revision that carries it, because the revision before 26f1d7e also has the derive-the-month write path that leaves the month total unchanged.
Keep derive_the_month off for every shopper until a revision carrying the fix is running: the flag read returned nothing, so its current state was not seen.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' stored this-month spend totals fell short of the purchases behind them. The spend-integrity check found {A1} of {A2} shopper totals not reconciling, the widest short by {A3}, with the oldest affected purchase recorded at {A4}. The monthly statement and the spend summary read that stored figure, so they show the short total.

Each current-month purchase recorded from the onset on was added to the account's purchases and to the lifetime total, but the stored total_this_month_cents was left where it was. The reconciliation compares that field with the sum of the current-month purchases, so the gap grew with every purchase.

ruled_out.what: The earlier deploy P1 of revision 4c810f2: the alert dates the oldest affected purchase at {A4}, after deploy P2 at {P2.1}, so no harm is dated while P1's revision ran alone.
A flag change: the flag provider's history showed {T14.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus in the {T14.3} hour before the onset.

causal_chain.step: Deploy P2 at {P2.1} put revision 26f1d7e into production, {began - P2.1} before the oldest affected purchase. As of {T11.1}, all {T11.2} replicas ran it. That revision took the month-total update out of record_purchase. At the same revision, record_purchase_deriving_the_month, which record_a_purchase uses when derive_the_month is true, also leaves the month total unchanged. So neither write path moved it.

The change rested on the idea that a shopper's month spend would be added up from the purchase history whenever it was needed, as its docstring says. But the code that uses the figure was not changed: the monthly statement divides and reads the stored total_this_month_cents, the spend summary divides it, and the reconciliation compares it. With nothing writing it any more, the stored copy went stale and every reader served or checked the stale figure.

input.cause_in_plain_words: A code change stopped the shop adding each new purchase to the shopper's running total for the current month, while the parts of the shop that show and check that total still read the stored figure, so it fell further behind what shoppers had actually bought.

contributing_factors.factor: The spend-integrity check, the only thing the record shows finding the fault, runs only every {A5} days, so stored month totals could drift for days before anything raised an alert.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A check run soon after each deploy, or often, would have found the shortfall soon after the onset, before most of the affected totals were written short.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No test or check was seen that records purchases through record_a_purchase and asserts that the stored month total still reconciles with the purchases, so a change dropping the month-total write could ship while readers still read the field.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test like that would have failed against revision 26f1d7e before it was deployed.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile paged nobody when it fired: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A paged person could have taken the recommended rollback and started the repair as soon as the alert fired, rather than the recommendation waiting for someone to notice it.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

contributing_factors.factor: Revision 26f1d7e was deployed to production from a branch that is not in main's history, so it reached production without being on main.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Had deploys been limited to revisions on main, 26f1d7e would not have shipped as it stood without first going through main.
contributing_factors.label: CF-4

got_lucky: The fault was found before the month it began in had ended, so the stored month totals can still be recomputed from this month's purchases. Code-Fix says that recomputation stops being right once the month rolls over.
went_well: Argus tied the onset to deploy P2 and read that deployment's diff {T10.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
Argus recommended the rollback rather than taking an action whose effect nothing would confirm within the time it waits.
Code-Fix proposed a draft pull request with a fix, tests and a repair script, PR #342, {T19.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
went_wrong: The Investigator put forward C1 and C2 as separate candidates, each with its own confidence, although both blame the same deploy of 26f1d7e and the same dropped month-total write.

The candidates looked only at record_purchase and missed that the derive-the-month write path also leaves the month total unchanged, so the recommended rollback alone would not stop the drift for shoppers on that path.
The only action recommended was the rollback, which leaves the totals already written short as they are. Only Code-Fix's repair script, which nothing has run, addresses them.

input.root_cause: Revision 26f1d7e took the month-total update out of record_purchase because its docstring held that a shopper's month spend would be added up from the purchase history whenever it was needed. But the monthly statement, the spend summary and the reconciliation all still read the stored total_this_month_cents. At that revision the other write path, record_purchase_deriving_the_month, also leaves the month total where it was, so whichever path the flag picked, every current-month purchase left the stored month total further below the purchases behind it.
input.still_at_risk: Revision 26f1d7e was still running on every replica, so each new current-month purchase would leave another stored month total further short for statements and spend summaries to read; rolling back would not correct the totals already written short, and the derive-the-month write path, which the earlier revision also carries, leaves the month total unchanged as well.
input.symptom: Shoppers' this-month spend totals fell short of the purchases behind them
